==Problem==
Mary chose an even <imath>4</imath>-digit number <imath>n</imath>. She wrote down all the divisors of <imath>n</imath> in increasing order from left to right: <imath>1,2,\ldots,\dfrac{n}{2},n</imath>. At some moment Mary wrote <imath>323</imath> as a divisor of <imath>n</imath>. What is the smallest possible value of the next divisor written to the right of <imath>323</imath>?

<imath>\textbf{(A) } 324 \qquad \textbf{(B) } 330 \qquad \textbf{(C) } 340 \qquad \textbf{(D) } 361 \qquad \textbf{(E) } 646</imath>

==Solution 1 (Inequalities)==

Let <imath>d</imath> be the next divisor written to the right of <imath>323.</imath>

If <imath>\gcd(323,d)=1,</imath> then <cmath>n\geq323d>323^2>100^2=10000,</cmath> which contradicts the precondition that <imath>n</imath> is a <imath>4</imath>-digit number.

It follows that <imath>\gcd(323,d)>1.</imath> Since <imath>323=17\cdot19,</imath> the smallest possible value of <imath>d</imath> is <imath>17\cdot20=\boxed{\textbf{(C) } 340},</imath> from which <cmath>n=\operatorname{lcm}(323,d)=17\cdot19\cdot20=6460.</cmath>
~MRENTHUSIASM ~tdeng

==Solution 2 (Inequalities)==

Let <imath>d</imath> be the next divisor written to the right of <imath>323.</imath>

Since <imath>n</imath> is even and <imath>323=17\cdot19,</imath> we have <imath>n=2\cdot17\cdot19\cdot k=646k</imath> for some positive integer <imath>k.</imath> Moreover, since <imath>1000\leq n\leq9998,</imath> we get <imath>2\leq k\leq15.</imath> As <imath>d>323,</imath> it is clear that <imath>d</imath> must be divisible by <imath>17</imath> or <imath>19</imath> or both.

Therefore, the smallest possible value of <imath>d</imath> is <imath>17\cdot20=\boxed{\textbf{(C) } 340},</imath> from which <cmath>n=\operatorname{lcm}(323,d)=17\cdot19\cdot20=6460.</cmath>
~MRENTHUSIASM ~bjhhar

==Solution 3 (Quick)==
The prime factorization of <imath>323</imath> is <imath>17 \cdot 19</imath>. Our answer must be a multiple of either <imath>17</imath> or <imath>19</imath> or both. Since <imath>17 < 19</imath>, the next smallest divisor that is divisble by <imath>17</imath> would be <imath>323 + 17 = \boxed{\textbf{(C) } 340}</imath>

~[https://artofproblemsolving.com/wiki/index.php/User:South South]

==Solution 4 (Answer Choices)==

Since prime factorizing <imath>323</imath> gives you <imath>17 \cdot 19</imath>, the desired answer needs to be a multiple of <imath>17</imath> or <imath>19</imath>, this is because if it is not a multiple of <imath>17</imath> or <imath>19</imath>, <imath>n</imath> will be more than a <imath>4</imath> digit number. For example, if the answer were to instead be <imath>324</imath>, <imath>n</imath> would have to be a multiple of <imath>2^2\cdot3^4\cdot17\cdot19</imath> for both <imath>323</imath> and <imath>324</imath> to be a valid factor, meaning <imath>n</imath> would have to be at least <imath>104652</imath>, which is too big. Looking at the answer choices, <imath>\textbf{(A)}</imath> and <imath>\textbf{(B)}</imath> are both not a multiple of neither <imath>17</imath> nor <imath>19</imath>, <imath>\textbf{(C)}</imath> is divisible by <imath>17</imath>. <imath>\textbf{(D)}</imath> is divisible by <imath>19</imath>, and <imath>\textbf{(E)}</imath> is divisible by both <imath>17</imath> and <imath>19</imath>. Since <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C) } 340}</imath> is the smallest number divisible by either <imath>17</imath> or <imath>19</imath> it is the answer. Checking, we can see that <imath>n</imath> would be <imath>6460</imath>, a <imath>4</imath>-digit number. Note that <imath>n</imath> is also divisible by <imath>2</imath>, one of the listed divisors of <imath>n</imath>. (If <imath>n</imath> was not divisible by <imath>2</imath>, we would need to look for a different divisor.)

-Edited by Mathandski

==Solution 5 (Answer Choices)==
Note that <imath>323</imath> multiplied by any of the answer choices results in a <imath>5</imath> or <imath>6</imath>-digit <imath>n</imath>. So, we need a choice that shares a factor(s) with <imath>323</imath>, such that the factors we'll need to add to the prime factorization of <imath>n</imath> (in result to adding the chosen divisor) won't cause our number to multiply to more than <imath>4</imath> digits. 
The prime factorization of <imath>323</imath> is <imath>17\cdot19</imath>, and since we know <imath>n</imath> is even, our answer needs to be 

* even 

* has a factor of <imath>17</imath> or <imath>19</imath>

We see <imath>340</imath> achieves this and is the smallest to do so (<imath>646</imath> being the other). So, we get <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C) } 340}</imath>.

==Solution 6 (Olympiad Proof )==
This is not the fastest solution, but if i saw this question on an Olympiad/AIME, where there are no answer choices, and my work counted, this is what i would do (for the purpose of this question, a=323, b=answer, c=the four digit number);

<imath>\newline</imath>
Note that for any <imath>a,b,c \in \mathbb{Z}^+</imath>, if <imath>a|c</imath> and <imath>b|c</imath> then lcm<imath>(a,b)|c</imath> (this is because if something divides a or b, it must divide c, and thus the max of all of the prime factors, ie: lcm, divides c) since <imath>a=323,b > a</imath>, if <imath>gcd(a,b)=1</imath> then <imath>lcm(a,b)=ab</imath> and thus <imath>ab|c \implies c>a^2 \implies c>100^2 \implies</imath> c is not a four digit number.
<imath>\newline</imath> thus, <imath>gcd(a,b)\neq1</imath>. This implies that either <imath>17|b</imath>, or <imath>19|b</imath>, or both.

<imath>\newline</imath> Case 1: <imath>17|b</imath>, <imath>19\not|b</imath>. We let <imath>b=17b'</imath>, and by Euclid's Lemma, <imath>19\not|b'</imath>. Then, <imath>lcm(323,b)|c \implies 17(lcm(19,b'))|c</imath>. Since we already established that, <imath>19\not|b</imath> (and since 19 is prime, if it does not divide a number it is coprime to that number), <imath>17*19*b'|c \implies 323b'|c</imath>. Since <imath>b=17b'>19*17</imath>, <imath>b' \geq 20</imath>. A quick check shows <imath>b'=20, b=340</imath> suffices.
<imath>\newline</imath> Now, let us show that there are no such numbers less than 340.
<imath>\newline</imath> Presume there exists such a number, <imath>n \in \mathbb{Z}^+</imath> is in the range <imath>(323,340)</imath>. By hypothesis, there is a <imath>d>1</imath> such that <imath>d|323</imath>, <imath>d|n</imath>. By properties of divisibility <imath>d|n-323</imath>. the maximum possible value of <imath>n-323</imath> is <imath>17^-</imath> (basically an arbitrary amount smaller than 17). But, since <imath>d>1</imath> and <imath>d|323, d \in \{17,19,323\}</imath>. Of which, the minimum value is d=17. but, <imath>17>17^-</imath> so there is no such d, and no such n.
<imath>\newline</imath> Thus, our answer is just <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C) } 340}</imath>.
<imath>\newline</imath> ~Stereotypicalmathnerd

==Solution 7==

Let the value of the next divisor be <imath>x</imath>. Then it follows that <imath>lcm(323,x)|n</imath>. For the sake of this problem, suppose <imath>lcm(323,x)=n</imath>, since it seems unlikely that <imath>lcm(323,x)\leq 4999</imath>. From here, there are two ways to solve this problem (note that <imath>323=17\times19)</imath>. <imath>\newline</imath>

<imath>\textbf{Ending 1.1 }</imath> 

You can simply prime factorize each answer choice and find one that will produce a valid value for <imath>n</imath>. <imath>\newline</imath>

<imath>\textbf{Ending 1.2 }</imath> 

Alternatively, if you know the identity relating <imath>gcd</imath> and <imath>lcm</imath> (<imath>gcd(a,b)\times lcm(a,b)=a\times b</imath>), this problem can be rewritten as <imath>gcd(323,x)\times lcm(323,x)=323\times x</imath>. Since <imath>lcm(323,x)=n</imath>, this means <imath>n=\frac{323\times x}{gcd(323,x)}</imath>.

Using either ending will produce the final answer of <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C) } 340}</imath> (This means <imath>n=\frac{323\times 340}{gcd(323,340)} \to n=\frac{17^2 \times 19 \times 20}{17} \to n=6460</imath>, which checks out).<imath>\newline</imath>

~pandapower24

==Solution 8==

The key point is that <imath>n</imath> is even. Also, <imath>323n < 10000 \implies n \leq 30</imath>. The key idea is that <imath>323 = 17 \cdot 19</imath>. If we were to divide by some <imath>n < 17</imath>, then dividing by 17 yields a smaller value, which is not allowed. Hence, consider <imath>n = 18</imath> in which <imath>19 \cdot 18 = 342</imath> is obtained. 

Now we check the next value, when <imath>n = 20</imath> so we can check 19. In that case, <imath>17 \cdot 20 = 340</imath> is formed.

We now prove no other values exist. Simply speaking, if <imath>n > 20</imath>, then consider <imath>323 \cdot n</imath>. If <imath>n</imath> is a prime, dividing by <imath>n</imath> gives 323, and the next number is anyways <imath>17 \cdot n</imath>. This however is minimized at <imath>n = 20</imath>, hence no cases arise. Similarly, if <imath>n</imath> is composite with a prime factorization, one can still rewrite it of the form <imath>323 \cdot n</imath>. But all prime factors of <imath>n</imath> are less than or equal to 15, hence the minimum is still at when we divide by 19, in which <imath>17 \cdot n</imath>. But this is still minimized at <imath>n = 20</imath>, hence no cases arise. <imath>\blacksquare</imath>

The answer is <imath>\boxed{340}</imath>, and we are done. <imath>\square</imath>

~Pinotation
